name: Alfredo Di Stéfano
milestone_by_age_26: Won Copa América 1947 with Argentina (scoring 6 goals in 6 games) and was top scorer of the 1947 Argentine Primera División with 27 goals for River Plate, all by age 21.
early_history_summary: Di Stéfano grew up in Buenos Aires playing street football, influenced by his father who had played for River Plate. He joined River Plate's youth team in 1944, debuted for the first team in 1945 at age 19, was loaned to Huracán in 1946, and returned to River Plate in 1947 to become the league's top scorer and win the Copa América with Argentina.
family_context_summary: Di Stéfano's father was a former River Plate defender who retired prematurely due to a knee injury in 1912. The family was of Italian-Argentine descent and lived in Barracas, a working-class neighborhood of Buenos Aires. His father introduced him to football and wrote a letter of recommendation to River Plate for his audition.
parent_family_domain_summary: Di Stéfano's father, Alfredo Sr., played for River Plate briefly in the 1913 League Championship. He introduced young Alfredo to football and facilitated his entry into River Plate's youth system through a letter of recommendation.
evidence_summary: Di Stéfano's father, a former River Plate player, introduced him to football and secured an audition at the club. He debuted for River Plate's first team at 19 in 1945, was loaned to Huracán in 1946 where he scored 10 goals in 25 games, and returned to River Plate in 1947 to become the league's top scorer (27 goals) and win the Copa América with Argentina (6 goals in 6 games). By 21 he was one of the best forwards in South American football.

family_context_summary: Del Piero's father was an electrician and his mother a housekeeper in Conegliano, a small town in the Veneto region. parent_family_domain_summary: Del Piero's brother Stefano briefly played professional football with Sampdoria, providing a family-domain model and motivation. His father was an electrician, not connected to professional football beyond Stefano's career.

name: Astor Piazzolla
milestone_by_age_26: Joined Aníbal Troilo's orchestra — one of the greatest tango orchestras of the era — as bandoneonist and arranger at age 18 (1939), and by 25 had formed his own Orquesta Típica and composed his first formal tango 'El Desbande' (1946).
early_history_summary: Piazzolla was given a bandoneon at age 8 in New York, made his first recording at 10, composed his first tango at 11, studied Bach with Hungarian pianist Béla Wilda, and appeared in a film with Carlos Gardel at 13. He returned to Argentina at 15, moved to Buenos Aires at 17, and joined Troilo's orchestra at 18, later studying classical composition with Alberto Ginastera.
family_context_summary: Piazzolla was the only child of Italian immigrant parents. His father Vicente was a barber who worked long hours in New York. The family lived in Greenwich Village and later Little Italy, both working-class immigrant neighborhoods. His father bought him a bandoneon from a pawn shop for $19 and played tango records at home.
parent_family_domain_summary: Piazzolla's father, a barber and Italian immigrant, bought him his first bandoneon from a pawn shop and exposed him to tango music through records of Carlos Gardel and Julio de Caro. The father's support was instrumental but not based on professional musical expertise.

The combination of mentorship (Wilda, Troilo, Ginastera), immersion in both New York jazz and Buenos Aires tango scenes, and extraordinary early reps made him an elite musician by his mid-20s.

name: Imre Kertész
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Kertész worked as a journalist and translator in his 20s but did not publish his first novel (Fatelessness/Sorstalanság) until 1975 at age 46. He gained widespread recognition only in the late 1980s and won the Nobel Prize in 2002.
early_history_summary: Kertész was deported to Auschwitz at 14 and Buchenwald at 15, was liberated in 1945, worked for a Budapest newspaper until dismissed in 1951, did military service, then supported himself as a freelance writer and translator of German-language authors. He began writing Fatelessness in 1960 but it took over a decade to complete.
family_context_summary: Kertész was born into a Jewish family in Budapest. No family writing or literary background documented. He was deported to Auschwitz at 14, which profoundly shaped his later work but did not constitute a literary milestone by 26.

name: Pete Best
milestone_by_age_26: Joined the Beatles as drummer in August 1960 at age 18, performed with them in Hamburg, and played on their first commercial recordings (Polydor sessions with Tony Sheridan, 1961) before being dismissed in August 1962.
early_history_summary: Best grew up in Liverpool where his mother Mona opened the Casbah Coffee Club in their cellar, hosting early performances by the Quarrymen (future Beatles). He played drums in his own band, the Black Jacks, at the Casbah before being recruited by Paul McCartney to join the Beatles for their first Hamburg trip in August 1960.
family_context_summary: Best was born in Madras, India, and moved to Liverpool as a child. His mother Mona Best opened the Casbah Coffee Club in their cellar, which became a significant venue for early Liverpool rock and roll. The club hosted some of the Quarrymen's (future Beatles) first performances.
parent_family_domain_summary: Best's mother Mona created the Casbah Coffee Club, a key venue in the early Liverpool music scene. This gave Pete direct access to the Beatles and the local music community, though Mona was not a musician herself.
evidence_summary: Best's mother opened the Casbah Coffee Club, giving him direct access to the Beatles and Liverpool's emerging music scene. He was recruited as the Beatles' drummer at 18 because he had his own drum kit and was available for Hamburg. He played on the band's first commercial recordings (Polydor, 1961) and performed extensively in Hamburg and Liverpool. However, the Beatles' global fame arrived after his dismissal in 1962, and his own success was modest.

name: Fernando Botero
milestone_by_age_26: Had his first solo exhibition at Galería Leo Matiz in Bogotá at age 19 (1951) and won second prize at the IX National Artists' Salon in Colombia at age 20 (1952) with 'Frente al Mar.'
early_history_summary: Botero grew up in Medellín in humble circumstances after his father died when he was 4. He published illustrations in El Colombiano newspaper at 16, worked as a set designer, moved to Bogotá at 19 for his first solo exhibition, and used prize money to study at the San Fernando Academy in Madrid and the San Marco Academy in Florence.
family_context_summary: Botero's father died when he was 4, leaving his mother, a seamstress, to raise the family with help from an uncle. The family had very humble means. His uncle sent him to a bullfighting school at 12, and Botero sold watercolors outside the bullring to fund his art.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No family artistic background noted. His uncle played a supportive role but was not an artist.

name: Glenn Gould
milestone_by_age_26: Made US debut recital at the Phillips Gallery in Washington, D.C. (January 2, 1955) at age 22, signed an exclusive Columbia Masterworks recording contract the next day, and released the landmark Goldberg Variations recording in 1956 (age 23-24), becoming an internationally renowned pianist.
early_history_summary: Gould showed perfect pitch at age 3, began piano lessons with his mother at 4, entered the Toronto Conservatory of Music at 10, earned his Associate diploma at 12, and studied with Chilean pianist Alberto Guerrero for 10 years. His US debut at 22 prompted a Columbia contract on the basis of a single performance, and his Goldberg Variations debut recording became one of the most celebrated classical recordings ever.
family_context_summary: Gould was the only child of Russell Herbert Gould, a successful Toronto furrier and amateur violinist, and Florence Greig Gould, a piano and organ teacher who claimed descent from Norwegian composer Edvard Grieg. Both parents were musical and his mother gave him his first piano lessons at age 4. The family was middle-class, able to afford conservatory training.
parent_family_domain_summary: Gould's mother was a piano and organ teacher who gave him his first lessons and continued teaching him for years. His father was an amateur violinist. His mother claimed a family connection to Edvard Grieg. The household was deeply musical, providing both domain expertise and early training.
